sections.title: Introduction
sections.html:
It goes without saying that nearly everybody on earth today has access to a web browser. The web is the defacto standard computing platform of the 21st century.

While Logo cousins Snap and Scratch have flourished on the web, Logo itself has languished. In my personal quest to hack on Logo programs on my phone I tried many broken "Logo" apps offering little power if they were even Logo at all.

Now thanks to Web Assembly you can run full UCB Logo right in your browser with beautful SVG turtle graphics, high quality animations, and JavaScript integration.

sections.title: Genuine article
sections.html: This is not some retro-nostalgic vibe-coded-slop version of Logo. This is Brian Harvey's original C-Logo interpreter hand-ported to Web Assembly with Emscripten by real humans®. Map, reduce, macros, they're all there. The terminal UI, barebones editor, and turtle graphics are a mix of C, JS, HTML, SVG, and CSS.

sections.title: Mobile-first design
sections.html:
Although UCB Logo Web Edition works great on desktop browsers, most people in the world don't own a computer, they own a phone. Priority is given to offering an outstanding mobile user experience. Mobile users need to use their OS native input widgets to edit tiny text with their big mushy fingers. If you've ever tried to SSH from a phone you know what I'm talking about. They don't even have arrow keys.

soft-keys are provided for common punction that's difficult to enter on the on-screen keyboard.

SVG scales nicely accross the huge range of display resolutions present in mobile devices.

sections.title: Accessibility status and roadmap
sections.html:
As a web app, Web Edition is expected to work with third-party screen readers. Terminal output can be read, but compatibility across the whole interface, including input, editing, controls, and turtle drawings, still needs testing. Standard HTML and SVG are useful foundations, but do not by themselves ensure that every workflow or the meaning of a drawing is accessible.

Separately, Web Edition currently offers spoken output using text-to-speech. The longer-term goal is an optional built-in screen reader that can do much more than speak output. It should complement, not replace or interfere with, third-party screen readers.

The roadmap below is planned work, not a claim that these capabilities already exist. Each stage should include keyboard-only checks and testing with people who use assistive technology.

See the accessibility project plan for priorities, dependencies, work packages, and acceptance criteria.

1. Audit and define support
  • Inventory every workflow: startup, dialogs, command entry and output, command history, autocomplete, soft keys, source editor, settings, file actions, and turtle drawings.
  • Test current behavior with representative screen readers and browsers. Record what works, where focus goes, and which announcements are missing; do not infer support from markup alone.
  • Publish a support matrix and prioritize blockers with blind and low-vision Logo users.
2. Make command input and editing accessible
  • Preserve native, labeled text input and textarea behavior so screen readers can announce focus, caret movement, selection, and user-entered text.
  • Make command submission, interpreter busy/stopped state, errors, and command completion discoverable without stealing focus or repeatedly interrupting speech.
  • Ensure command history can be browsed and selected by keyboard and assistive technology, with the selected command returned to the input field predictably.
  • Make autocomplete announce suggestions, selection, and dismissal. Verify keyboard and screen-reader operation for both the command line and editor.
  • Make soft-key insertion announce the inserted character when appropriate, restore focus to the edited field, and preserve the caret and selection.
  • Provide a usable multiline editor workflow, including navigation, selection, applying changes, and reporting errors. Avoid duplicating the screen reader's configured character/word echo; any optional Logo speech or command readback must be separately controllable and non-interfering.
3. Verify and improve third-party screen-reader access
  • Give every control a correct accessible name, role, state, and keyboard behavior; verify dialogs, focus entry/restoration, settings, uploads/downloads, and status/error announcements.
  • Make terminal output reviewable and navigable, including new output, prompts, partial lines, and long sessions. Keep announcements useful rather than speaking the entire output stream repeatedly.
  • Define an accessible representation for turtle graphics: a concise drawing summary and a navigable description of meaningful objects/actions, with a way to inspect coordinates, labels, colors, and drawing order where applicable. A single SVG image label is not sufficient for complex drawings.
  • Ensure animation can be paused or stopped and does not cause a constant stream of disruptive announcements. Respect reduced-motion preferences.
4. Develop a built-in screen reader
  • Design an optional reader for the Web Edition itself that goes beyond spoken output: read and review input, output, controls, focus and state, editor content, and available turtle-drawing descriptions.
  • Provide keyboard-accessible navigation and on-demand review, with adjustable voice, rate, verbosity, typing echo, and a way to interrupt or silence speech. Make the reader discoverable and operable without relying on visual cues.
  • Keep it independently controllable and avoid duplicate speech or conflicting shortcuts when a third-party screen reader is in use. Continue exposing standard browser accessibility semantics regardless of whether it is enabled.
  • Test realistic workflows with blind users, including startup, editing, execution, errors, dialogs, and drawings. Document what the built-in reader can and cannot access; it does not replace system-wide assistive technology.
5. Add non-color visual modes
  • Add selectable drawing palettes for common color-vision deficiencies, using distinguishable hues and luminance rather than hue alone.
  • Add a grayscale palette and verify that important lines, fills, and regions remain distinguishable when printed or viewed without color.
  • Add a black-and-white SVG pattern mode that maps Logo color indices to distinguishable vector patterns, line styles, and/or markers instead of relying on color. Cover both strokes and fills, keep patterns legible at different zoom levels, and preserve them in downloaded SVG files.
  • Make palette selection available by keyboard and screen reader, provide a visible indication of the active mode, and do not silently change Logo's underlying color semantics or existing drawings.
  • Validate palettes with color-vision simulations as an early check, then with grayscale output and users; simulations alone are not acceptance evidence.
6. Assess braille compatibility
  • Test the complete command-entry and output workflow through screen readers paired with refreshable braille displays, including command editing, history, autocomplete, errors, and changing output.
  • Determine whether the SVG drawing summary and detailed descriptions are understandable and navigable on braille displays, and document browser and screen-reader limitations.
  • Consult braille and tactile-graphics users about whether a structured text description, downloadable SVG, or a separate tactile-graphics export would best serve drawing inspection. Treat tactile output as a research question, not an assumed capability of browser SVG or braille displays.
7. Verify and maintain
  • Add automated checks for accessible names/roles, focus order, keyboard operation, live-region behavior, and palette/export correctness.
  • Run manual acceptance with current supported screen reader/browser combinations, including desktop and mobile, and record actual versions and tested hardware. Include users of screen readers, magnification, color-vision adaptations, and braille where available.
  • Keep accessibility behavior and known limitations in this document current as features ship; do not describe a planned or automated check as verified assistive-technology support.

sections.title: New features
sections.html:
Scalable Vector Graphics provide stunning and responsive turtle art independent of the native display resolution. SVG turtle art can be easily printed, saved, shared, or opened in another program. The turtle shape can also be drawn with SVG with makesprite.

Web Edition features an exclusive real-time animation facility (experimental).

Use the JS interop to break the limits of logo and manipulate DOM directly or access cutting edge web APIs.

sections.title: Differences and missing features
sections.html: While we claim "100% compatibility", we are missing a few minor features available in other UCB Logo builds. They have no effect on the core Logo language.

sections.title: Missing or non-functioning words:
sections.html:
Most of these are planned to be added.

Terminal emulation related words
  • standout
  • setcursor
  • cursor
  • setmargins
  • settextcolor
  • increasefont
  • decreasefont
  • settextsize
  • textsize
  • setfont
  • settextfont
  • font

The terminal is currently "dumb". Emulation features are planned.

Graphics words
  • scrunch (uneeded with SVG)
  • setscrunch
  • fill (flood-fill; we do support filled)
  • refresh (uneeded with SVG)
  • norefresh
  • savepict (but see SVG export)
  • loadpict (use JS to add whatever to the drawing)
  • epspict (again see SVG export)
Misc words
  • shell (works in node.js, but not in browser)

There is no shell word in web browsers since there is no shell on the web. We provide runjs as an alternative. We do not plan to add a shell, but it might be possible to do so with WASI. shell works normally in node.js.

sections.title: Virtual filesystem
sections.html:
Web apps cannot access the host filesystem so UCB Logo includes a persistent internal virtual filesystem. This allows file-related words to function otherwise normally and allows users to save and load their programs.

Warning: Logo must be installed as an app to ensure reliable long term data persistence.

Warning: Browsers may evict saved Logo files. Chrome/Edge/FF use an LRU policy and only start to evict data when the user's storage volume fills up. Safari always evicts data after 7 days of non-usage.

Always back up your data. Use the "Download Logo Session" button.

Future releases may integrate with cloud storage, e.g. Google Drive.

`penerase``

Historically Logo drew bitmaps. While SVG is vastly superior in nearly every respect, there is one thing bitmaps can do that SVG can't; erasing.

We emulate erasing by drawing on a mask layer to reveal the background. So nothing is really erased, but it looks like it is. It's close but not pixel-perfect.

UCB Logo historically supports a proprietary vector art file format by the unfortunate name of PICT. It's basically a serialized list of turtle commands. PICT words might still work but I haven't tried it.

wait

Waits are interrupted if an event arrives, so the wait time should be taken as a maximum wait time rather than a guaranteed wait time.

This was necessitated by the fact that Asyncified C programs are non-reentrant and we have no signals or any other way of asynchronously responding to events in C.

We have to wake Logo up so it can poll the events from the event queue, or they will not be handled until the (potentially very long) wait timeout. This is particularly important for STOP events but also relevant to mouse clicks etc.

This is important to ensure adequate responsiveness in existing Logo programs, like mines, which idle in a wait loop assuming events will be handled asynchronously.

sections.title: As a web page
sections.html: UCB Logo can run in recent versions of most popular browsers including Chrome, Edge, Firefox, and Safari, and also on Androind and iOS mobile devices.

sections.title: As a progressive web app
sections.html:
UCB Logo can also be installed as an app on most mobile devices by selecting "Add to Home" from your mobile browser menu.

Installed as an app, UCB Logo features full-offline capabilities and persistant storage on it's virtual filesystem.

sections.title: Help dialog
sections.html:
Open Help with the toolbar Help button, the Help button in the editor dialog, or F1. The Words tab lists Logo words by category; select a word to read its usage and description. The User manual and Web Edition tabs hold the full documents. Search covers words and documents. Insert adds the selected word and a space at the caret in the command input, or in the editor when the editor dialog is open; Insert and close also closes Help.

The manual and Web Edition documents load in the background after startup, so they are available offline only after one online session.

sections.title: Web-edition exclusive words
sections.html:
Experimental, subject to change, may crash Logo

  • animationstart
  • animationstop
  • animationframact
  • animationtime
  • animationdelay
  • makesprite
  • setturtlesprite
  • setshaperendering
  • runjs
  • runLogo (JS Function)
  • tone
  • speak
  • setspeechvoice
  • setspeechlang
  • setspeechrate
  • setspeechpitch
  • `speakoutput
Animation words

Exclusive to Web Edition is an animation facility based on the HTMl5 requestAnimationFrame API. This enables Logo to render smooth turtle-graphics based animations at 60fps or higher on modern devices. Further, because the loop runs asynchronously via Logo "actions", Logo remains available for live interactive animation development.

Normally when SVG is animated the browser renders the vectors to bitmaps and transforms them on the GPU. This is very fast. This also has the side effect of introducing ugly pixelated visual artifacts in line-art.

When we use turtle graphics to draw each full animation frame from scratch we effectively de-optimize the browser's SVG rendering pipeline by forcing the browser to rerender the SVG for each frame. This improves visual quality at the cost of somewhat increased CPU usage.

To set an animation frame action

make "animationact [words to draw frame]

To get the total time the loop has been running

:animationtime

To get the time since the last frame

:animationdelta

To start animation loop

animationstart

To stop animation loop

animationstop

Example:

cs pu
make "animationact [setheading towards mousepos fd :animationdelta * 0.2]
animationstart

The turtle should start smoothly chasing your mouse pointer around the screen at a constant speed.

Sprite words

Sprites are another web-exclusive feature. Right now there is only one sprite: the turtle. So basically this is just an SVG-based alternative to setturtleshape. Support for multiple sprites is planned. It's... unclear what the actual difference between a sprite and a turtle even is, it's not like we're using real hardware NTSC sprites... This abstraction needs more thought.

To create a new sprite, first clearscreen and draw it with the turtle, then

makesprite "spritename

The drawing will be captured and saved in "spritename and cleared from the screen. This process can be repeated to prepare additional sprite shapes.

To set the turtle to a sprite shape

setturtlesprite "spritename
SVG Rendering Control Words

Sets the SVG shape rendering mode in CSS. In practice this just turns anti-aliasing on or off, don't get too excited.

To set the SVG shape rendering mode

setshaperendering "crispedges

Accepted words are

  1. "geometricprecision Default; enables anti-aliasing
  2. "optimizespeed Typically identical to 1
  3. "crispedges Disables anti-aliasing

This can also be changed in the settings dialog.

Color theme

The web edition follows the browser or operating system color preference by default. Choose System, Light, or Dark in the settings dialog, or use the Logo word setdarkmode with "system, "light, or "dark. This choice is saved between sessions. settextcolor overrides the theme colors.

Audio tone word

tone freq duration

Plays a damped sine wave tone at the specified frequency for the specified duration. Playback is asynchronous so to play a song insert waits.

tone 440 60

Plays a 440hz tone (A440 pitch) for 60 ticks or 1 second.

tone 440 60 wait 60 tone 440 60

Plays two notes sequentially.

tone 220 60 tone 440 60

Plays A-440 and A-220 notes simultaneously, a simple chord.

Text-to-speech

getvoices

Returns a list of available [voice lang] pairs.

setspeechvoice

Sets the speech voice. Voice names are case-sensitive so use v-bars.

setspeechvoice "|Bubbles|

setspeechlang "|en-US|

It is not necessary to set the speech language unless it differs from your browser's default.

setspeechpitch 1.0

Set speech pitch. 1.0 is the default. Recommend changing in 0.1 increments.

setspeechrate 1.0

Set speech rate. 1.0 is the default. Recommend changing in 0.1 increments.

setspeakoutput

Speak logo console output as printed.

(setspeakoutput "false)

Do not speak logo output.

Experimental Logo/JS interoperation

Call JavaScript from Logo and Logo from JavaScript or both at once using UCB Logo's JavaScript Foreign Function Interface.

To call JavaScript from Logo
runjs "|console.log('Called JS from Logo')|

Warning: Uses JS eval() so totally insecure and slow.

Communication is over standard IO so everything must be stringified. JS values are encoded to Berkeley Logo Object Notation or BLON. It's basically Logo JSON.

Bools, numbers, null, and undefined are stringified and vbarred. Strings are escaped and vbarred.

JS arrays are coerced to Logo sentences (cons lists, really).

JS objects are coerced to a list in Logo plist format which is a normal list but odd indices are keys and evens are values. The ordering may or may not be significant, it's up to the JS object. For objects with only a few keys a linear search is probably the fastest access. Otherwise load them into a Logo property list for keyed access; see example below.

ignore cascade [empty? ?] [pprop "myplist first ? first butfirst ? butfirst butfirst ?] parse runjs "|/* js func call that returns an object */|

No efforts are made to preserve semantics, e.g. JS null becomes Logo null, not NIL. This avoids the question of whether undefined should also be NIL or how to represent false. Interpretation of these values is up to the Logo program.

The resulting string is sent to Logo over stdin. It will be immediately evaluated by Logo, unless you do something with it, like print or parse or ignore it. JS and Logo both show their Lisp heritage here.

For more control over Logo/JS interaction it's not hard to add a new builtin word to Logo in C that wraps JavaScript using the Emscripten API. Suggestions are appreciated.

Examples:

? pr runjs "|(()=>true)()|
true
? pr runjs "|(()=>null)()|
null
? pr runjs "|(()=>undefined)()|
undefined
? pr runjs "|(()=>123)()|
123
? pr runjs "|(()=>123.456)()|
123.456
? pr runjs "|(()=>['hello', 'world'])()|
|hello| |world|
? show parse runjs "|(()=>['hello', 'world'])()|
[hello world]
? pr  runjs "|(()=>({hello: "world", foo: {poo: "bar", boo: ['bee', 42]}}))()|
|hello| |world| |foo| [|poo| |bar| |boo| [|bee| 42]]
? show runparse runjs "|(()=>({hello: "world", foo: {poo: "bar", boo: ['bee', 42]}}))()|
[hello world foo [poo bar boo [bee 42]]]
? ignore cascade [empty? ?] [pprop "pplist first ? first butfirst ? butfirst butfirst ?] parse runjs "|(()=>({hello: "world", foo: {poo: "bar", boo: ['bee', 42]}}))()|
? popl "pplist
Pprop "pplist "foo [poo bar boo [bee 42]]
Pprop "pplist "hello "world
To call Logo from Javascript
runLogo('pr [Called Logo from JS]')

Logo output

? Called Logo from JS
?

Setting the optional second argument to true causes Logo to echo the command

runLogo('pr [Called Logo from JS]', true)

Logo output

? pr [Called Logo from JS]
Called Logo from JS
?

No marshaling is provided as of now.

Warning: Also uses eval, the logo version. Logo commands are sent via stdin to the main eval loop. Totally insecure.

Ouroboros

I don't know why you would want to do this.

? ignore runjs "|setTimeout(()=>runLogo('pr [called Logo from JS from Logo]'),0)|
? called Logo from JS from Logo
?

Or this.

> runLogo(`ignore runjs "|console.log('called JS from Logo from JS')|`, true)
called JS from Logo from JS

sections.title: Background
sections.html:
In order to be able to run non-javascript software in web browsers, the Web has grown a standardized byte-code virtual stack machine more or less equivalent to the Java Virtual Machine. This VM specification is known as Web Assembly, or WASM.

WASM is a low-level virtual machine that does 3 main things

  1. Execute WASM bytecode on the virtual processor
  2. Expose virtual memory to WASM programs
  3. Facilitate interaction between WASM programs and the browser (HTML/JS/CSS etc)

WASM does NOT provide an operating system or a runtime or libraries or really much of anything else. As a platform it's similar to bare-metal. This was intentional to enable it to be a generic computing platform capable of running arbitrary software including full system emulators and desktop operating systems.

In the case of ucblogo we want to be able to run it in a browser without a heavyweight operating system. Further while WASM is very low level, the browser provides most of the facilities of a traditional OS; how else would chromebooks work? But the browser functionality is hidden behind the JavaScript Web API which is completely different from the POSIX API used by ucblogo.

Enter Emscripten; a system for porting UNIX software to the web. The Emscripten SDK includes a C/C++->WASM compiler based on clang/llvm and a fairly robust implementation of POSIX as a runtime library on top of the web browser's native API. This allows most UNIX programs to be ported to the web with minor changes.

sections.title: Asyncify
sections.html:
There is one major wrinkle; the web browser is a cooperative-multitasking environment; all programs must periodically yield to the browser event loop. But C programs execute synchronously. Without accounting for this long running C programs will freeze up the browser and you're gonna have a bad time. It's well known fact that JS copied this model from Classic MacOS.

But there is another major wrinkle; UCB Logo uses a generationl mark & sweep garbage collector to manage it's memory. This requires access to the stack and VM registers to scan for pointers. Sadly the registers are opaque to C and the stack is opaque to both C and WASM.

Asyncify solves both of these problems for us.

Firstly, Asyncify magically transforms synchronous C programs into asynchronous callbacks so your C function can await a JavaScript promise without blocking.

To do this Asyncify implements a shadow C stack in WASM linear memory, where the heap lives. This is addition to the opaque WASM stack. Asyncify unwinds and saves the stack whenever an async call is made. This includes spilling WASM registers into the c shadow stack.

This has the upshot of giving us a mechanism to scan these otherwise opaque memory regions.

Still Logo must ensure that it does an await every 50ms minimum no matter what it's doing in order to YIELD to the browser event loop and not block user interaction or cause unresponsive page alerts.

Logo must also yield after DOM mutations, like printing to the terminal or drawing turtle graphics, so the browser can render the changes. Logo must also yield to receive incoming events from JavaScript.

YIELD needs to be sprinkled around the code. It's particularly important to call it periodically from within long running loops, like parsing and evaluation loops.

The suggested way to do this is periodically check the wall clock and YIELD if we've passed some deadline, say 5ms. But checking the wall clock from WASM is pretty expensive so you don't want to do it often. But since you can't know exactly how long Logo will take between clock checks, you have to check it pretty often.

UCB Logo uses a heuristic approach whereby we call YIELD frequently, but we make those calls practically free by not actually yelding most of the time. Most calls to YIELD just decrement a counter and return. YIELD only checks the wall clock when the counter reaches zero, and then only yields if the deadline has passed, otherwise is just resets the counter. The result is reliable yielding with practically zero runtime cost.

On supporting browsers Logo yields uses the new scheduler.yield rather than setTimeout; this results in a significant peformance improvement.

Logo users can force a YIELD with the wait word. The wait will be interrupted if an event arrives.

Logo is fully asynchronous and does not use any polling loops, which results in excellent responsiveness, low CPU overhead, and extended battery life. The animation loop, when running, will impact battery life.

Logo executes as a "terminate and stay resident" or TSR program; the main() function returns, but the runtime stays alive so JavaScript can call into the Logo C API and run the evaluator. This permits a limited form of reentrency. True reentrency is prohibited by Asyncify as it will corrupt the shadow stack. JSPI solves this problem but it's unclear if it will work with our garbage collector, TBD. WASM-GC would eliminate this concern but is not currently supported by LLVM.

sections.title: Prerequisites
sections.html:
• Emscripten >= 4.5 https://emscripten.org/docs/getting_started/downloads.html
  • Python >= 3.6
  • Node.js >= 20

Emscripten will install it's own version of clang called emcc.

Note: Our makehelp target doesn't work with emscripten and must be built with a native toolchain.

sections.title: Building
sections.html:
The short version

cd ucblogo-code
. ~/emsdk/emsdk_env.sh
npm install
npm run build:web

sections.title: Runnning
sections.html:
Once compiled to WASM, ucblogo can be run in any WASM VM including node.js and any modern web browser using a local web server, e.g.

Running in browser

To debug the web app install the Chrome DWARF plugin and be sure to split debug symbols into ucblogo.debug.wasm. Always split debug symbols into a separate file. The combined file is too big and the touchy DWARF plugin will silently fail.

Emscripten includes a utility called emrun which will automatically start a little web server, open the program in a browser window, and pipe the javascript console output back to the terminal session. This requires that the --emrun flag was passed to the linker.

emrun ucblogo.html

There's also an experimental AI generated develoment server; it just serves up the local dir an includes CORS headers.

node webserver.js
emrun ucblogo.html

or

python3 -m http.server 8080 & xdg-open http://localhost:8080/ucblogo.html

or

node ./webserver.js & xdg-open http://localhost:8080/ucblogo.html

which inludes CORS headers for cross-site scripting.

Running in Node
node ./ucblogo-node.js

Logo terminal input is currently broken in node, but you can still use it to run unit tests from the console.

To debug in node I recommend using the official VSCode node debug plugin from MS.

You can also use Chrome dev tools to remotely debug Node but it leaves some things to be desired. Again you need the DWARF plugin.

sections.title: Debugging
sections.html:
The debugging experience is a mixed bag. On the one hand Chrome Devtools is a pretty amazing debugger. OTOH there is a huge impedance mismatch between C and the web. And errors that occur in JS don't necessarily include a C backtrace, or maybe the trace refers to assembly code an not C.

In the face of a difficult Logo bug, I recommend attempting to reproduce and fix it in a native WX Logo environment, then port the fix to the WASM build. gdb offers a much more powerful C debugging experience than chrome dev tools.

GC bugs can sometimes be forced to the surface by setting a tiny SEG_SIZE, like 8. The resultant GC thrashing has a fuzzing effect and will make existing bugs crash logo earlier and more often, which is good for debugging hard to reproduce bugs.

See also address-sanitizer.txt for how to turn on LLVM sanitizers.

See also contrib/gdb.rc for some useful GDB macros.

sections.title: Deployment
sections.html:
Releases are published automatically. Tag the commit that passed CI and push the tag:

git tag -m pXX pXX
git push origin pXX

The Deploy Web workflow then:

  1. Checks that git describe --tags --always --dirty equals the pushed tag.
  2. Builds and runs the full test suite with npm test (Emscripten pinned in the workflow to the same version as ci.yaml).
  3. Stages the site with npm run stage:web, which copies only the files the app needs, drops stale Workbox runtimes, and verifies that the sw.js precache revisions match the staged bytes and that the build embeds the tag in its version string.
  4. Commits the result to the gh_pages branch as pXX and pushes it. GitHub Pages serves that branch.

No amend or second build is needed: build outputs are not tracked, and sw.js is rebuilt after ucblogo.html by the normal make dependencies. Never re-tag a published release; the version string comes from the tag.

To publish by hand, build after tagging and stage into a gh_pages checkout:

npm run build:web
npm run stage:web -- ~/ucblogo-code-gh-pages --expect-version pXX

then commit and push in that checkout. The workflow's manual run (Actions > Deploy Web > Run workflow) does everything except publish and uploads the staged site as an artifact; GitHub only offers manual runs for workflows on the default branch.

Impact on the wx release process

The wx build is largely unaffected:

  • git.c (the git id in the version string) is only generated with --enable-gitid, which defaults to yes for --enable-wasm and no otherwise. It now uses git describe --tags --always --dirty, so a --enable-gitid wx build also shows lightweight tags and a -dirty suffix when tracked files are modified. Exact-tag builds still read (pXX).
  • makefile.msys (the Windows/MinGW build) has its own git describe rule and was not changed, so it does not add --tags or -dirty.
  • make clean also removes sw.js.map and the hash-named workbox-*.js and map files. .gitignore now ignores web-config.js, workbox-????????.js, /config.guess, and /config.sub; none of these were tracked or distributed.
  • The stale tracked workbox-*.js runtimes were removed from git.
  • The Deploy Web workflow runs for tags matching p[0-9]*, but only on commits that contain the workflow file. Once it is on master, any pNN tag, including a wx-only release, will also build and publish the web site. Use a different tag prefix or add a gate if that is not wanted.

sections.title: Future Directions
sections.html:
WASM-GC looks great, but LLVM hasn't picked it up yet.

Objective Logo would enable better JS object integration; they're both prototypal!

The UI/UX could use a lot of work, it's currently very MVP.

A hosted web service to backup and share logo programs.

Expose more JS APIs, like sensors.

Unicode would be nice.

Safari needs more testing.
